analysis.one_liner: Boosts IRS funding to audit high earners and corporations, with tougher penalties for the wealthiest taxpayers.
analysis.headline: The bill received no hearing, markup, or vote in the Senate Finance Committee and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would give the IRS a dedicated $31.5 billion each year, adjusted for inflation, to hire auditors, improve taxpayer service, and replace outdated technology. It directs enforcement toward taxpayers with incomes over $1 million and large corporations, raises underpayment penalties to as much as 40% for people making over $5 million, requires banks to report account flow data so the IRS can find unreported income, and lets the government use false-claims penalties against taxpayers making over $10 million who file false statements costing more than $1 million.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers. People who pay what they owe benefit when the tax gap shrinks, because honest filers effectively subsidize those who underreport. The bill also funds phone assistance, low-income taxpayer clinics, and help for seniors, and it requires the IRS to report annually on audit plans, the tax gap, and whether audits are racially skewed.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Compliant taxpayers, especially low- and middle-income filers

how_it_helps.text: The bill appropriates $31.5 billion per year for IRS taxpayer services, enforcement, and business systems modernization, with at least half going to enforcement and at least 15% to taxpayer services [S3].

It directs the IRS to shift audit resources toward high-income, high-wealth individuals and corporations and to report to Congress annually on that plan, on the tax gap, and on any racial disparities in enforcement [S2][S3].
It raises accuracy-related underpayment penalties from 20% to 30% for taxpayers with taxable income over $2 million and to 40% over $5 million, with matching increases in related penalties [S2][S3].
It bars the IRS from spending any of the new funds on private tax-debt collection contracts [S3].

analysis.who_pays: High-income and high-wealth taxpayers and large corporations, who would face more audits and higher penalties, and banks, which would have to report monthly account inflows and outflows for the accounts they hold — costs that could be passed on to customers through fees.

drawbacks.text: The bill requires covered financial institutions to report monthly gross inflows and outflows for every account they maintain, including personal accounts, which raised privacy objections and adds compliance costs likely to reach customers [S3].

The higher 30% and 40% penalty tiers are set by income level and apply to accuracy-related underpayments regardless of the taxpayer's intent, so an honest mistake by a very high earner would cost substantially more [S3].

More money does not guarantee results: the bill's own goals are advisory, and past IRS technology modernization efforts have run over budget and behind schedule, so the appropriation could be spent without the audit gains it promises [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary taxpayers the upside is large: fewer people getting away with underreported income, better IRS service, and a public record of where enforcement dollars go. The costs fall on a narrow group — very high earners, big corporations, and banks — plus a real but limited privacy trade-off from bank account reporting. On balance the bill is designed to shift the tax burden's honesty requirement toward those most able to game it, though its success would depend on the IRS actually hiring skilled auditors and modernizing successfully.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the Restoring the IRS Act on May 24, 2021 [S1][S5].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day, the only action it ever received [S5].
It drew one Democratic cosponsor and no Republicans [S4].
The Finance Committee took no further action, and the bill expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-income taxpayers and large corporations kept the status quo: no added audits, no higher penalties, and no new bank reporting that could expose unreported income. Banks and private tax-debt collection firms also avoided new requirements.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wealthy taxpayers, banks, and collection contractors

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and pursued its referral to the Finance Committee

against.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it without a path to the floor

sides.party_line_note: No roll call ever occurred; the bill's only support was one Democratic sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor, and it drew no Republican backing.

industries.industry: High-income and high-wealth taxpayers and large corporations
industries.note: The bill targets enforcement at filers with incomes over $1 million, raises underpayment penalties to as much as 40% for incomes over $5 million, and exposes very large taxpayers to false-claims penalties. The status quo — a large tax gap borne by compliant filers — is what this group gained from the bill's failure.

Banks would face new, recurring reporting duties on monthly account inflows and outflows for accounts they hold, a compliance cost likely to reach customers through fees. Their interest in avoiding the reporting ran against the public's interest in closing the tax gap.

The bill prohibits the IRS from using any of its funds for qualified private tax collection contracts, which pay collectors a share of what they extract from taxpayers. The bill's failure preserved those contracts.
